Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, this appraisal is hard to reconcile with the likely role in the trauma. A child witness may feel guilty, but 'I should have protected others' implies a level of responsibility and agency that is clinically implausible enough to question for this trauma context. The rest of the profile coheres around fear, helplessness, fragmented sensory memory, and hypervigilant threat monitoring; this single appraisal stands out as inconsistent with the demographics/trauma role.

vignette: When Malik was eight years old, the domestic violence in the adjacent apartment shattered his understanding of safety. He remembers the precise moment the shouting began, the splintering of a chair back, and the sharp glint of a kitchen knife caught in the hallway light. What frightened him most was the sudden, suffocating silence that followed-the kind of quiet that always preceded a blow he knew was coming. His young body had locked against the cold plaster, pressing into the corner just to keep still. That night etched itself into him as a series of frozen snapshots; even now, he recalls the scene not as a continuous narrative, but as a few stark pictures in his mind, each one carrying the full weight of the original terror. Now eighteen and working as a patrol officer, Malik navigates a world that constantly reactivates those early imprints. He walks the same familiar beat daily because he had come to believe he could not rely on himself to assess an unfamiliar area for danger. During a foot patrol near the precinct's eastern sector, he found himself tracing the edges of every parked vehicle for hidden objects, his gaze locked on potential weapons or dangerous objects whenever his eyes drifted from the sidewalk. Whenever he feels a baseline of discomfort or notices someone acting suspiciously on the street, his mind instantly pulls him back to the neighbor's kitchen. Those involuntary intrusions are accompanied by a physical jolt; his posture mimics the exact position he held as a child, and the overwhelming grief that surfaces leaves him breathless. His conviction that he is going crazy, combined with his fear that he is utterly helpless to stop bad things from happening, makes him hypersensitive to ordinary cues. Because he doubts his own stability, he interprets every glance and every shift in tone as a prelude to violence. This self-doubt fuels a relentless cycle. The intrusive memories themselves seem to dictate his reactions, causing him to flinch at sudden movements or feel entirely unprepared when a colleague pats his shoulder unexpectedly. Once those memories surface, they transform his present environment, making him fixate on potential weapons or dangerous objects wherever he walks. His constant vigilance against perceived danger, in turn, keeps the old memories fresh, ensuring they never fade into the background. Living in a state of constant alarm eroded his confidence further, reinforcing the thought that he was helpless to protect anyone, including himself. Because he feels so powerless, he avoids stepping into unknown precincts or detours, since navigating uncharted territory strips away his ability to track danger. The more he isolates himself in familiar zones, the more his mind waits for disaster, which in turn makes him more sensitive to any hint of unpredictability. His score of 77 on the standardized inventory mirrored the intensity of this daily hyperarousal. By the time he sought help, his routine had collapsed; he could no longer complete full shifts without leaving early, and his emotional withdrawal from his partner had drawn a formal command warning. He came to the clinic hoping to quiet the grief, to steady his hands, and to find a way to live without bracing for the next blow.
